title: A close read of the sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) paper: thousands of experts, only a few active at a time, massive parameters, near-constant compute
summary: An MoE layer holds many expert networks; a gating network selects only the top k for each input to compute. Total parameters and per-input compute are decoupled—the paper reaches 137 billion parameters. We work through Top-K gating, expert batching, and the load-balancing losses by hand, then look at the language modeling and translation experiments and how the idea made its way into Transformers and today's large models.
ai_summary: "Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer" (Shazeer et al., Google Brain, ICLR 2017) introduces a sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer: many feed-forward expert networks plus a noisy Top-K gating network, where each input is processed by only the selected experts. The paper scales expert batch size by mixing data and model parallelism, makes expert hidden layers larger to reduce communication overhead, and adds importance and load losses to stop the gate from favoring a few experts. With similar compute, language model perplexity drops sharply as expert count grows, and the MoE layer reaches about 137 billion parameters; in machine translation it beats GNMT while using less compute.
brief: Problem: more parameters make models stronger, but a conventional network uses all of its parameters for every example, so compute grows roughly quadratically with scale.
Method: an MoE layer combines many experts with a noisy Top-K gate; each input only runs through k experts, backed by mixed parallelism and load-balancing losses.
Result: with compute held constant, more experts give lower perplexity; on a 100-billion-word corpus, a 68-billion-parameter model cuts perplexity by 39%; translation beats GNMT with less compute.
Limitations: load balancing relies on extra loss terms; distributed communication and efficiency issues remain; some translation experiments use a different gate.

paper.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
paper.authors: Noam Shazeer, Azalia Mirhoseini, Krzysztof Maziarz, Andy Davis, Quoc Le, Geoffrey Hinton, Jeff Dean

cover.headline: A close read of the original MoE paper

nodes.label: Gate selects only the top-k experts

sections.h: The bottom line: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In January 2017, Noam Shazeer, Azalia Mirhoseini, Krzysztof Maziarz, Andy Davis, Quoc Le, Geoffrey Hinton, and Jeff Dean of Google Brain released this paper with a deliberately bold title: "Outrageously Large Neural Networks." It later appeared at ICLR 2017.

It tackles a fundamental tension: more parameters can hold more knowledge, but a conventional network has to use **all** of them for every example. As model size and data grow together, compute grows roughly as the product of the two. The paper's answer is **conditional computation**: each example activates only a small part of the network.

The specific mechanism is the **sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer (MoE)**: many small feed-forward networks with identical architecture but independent parameters, called "experts," plus a trainable "gating network." For each input, the gate selects only a few experts (say, 4) to compute, combines their outputs by weight, and leaves the rest completely unused.

Expert counts can therefore grow into the thousands, total parameters explode, and per-example compute stays nearly flat. The paper inserts the MoE layer between two LSTM layers, reaches 137 billion parameters, and beats the best results of the time on language modeling and machine translation while using less compute.

What makes it practical is a set of engineering fixes: how to give each expert a large enough batch, how to reduce communication between machines, and how to keep the gate from always favoring a few experts. Today's large MoE models still face the same problems.

callout.title: In one sentence
callout.text: MoE = many experts + a gate that keeps only the top k. Total parameters and per-input compute are decoupled: the model can be outrageously large while each token costs only a small slice of compute. The tradeoff is trickier load balancing and distributed communication.

callout.title: Three small concepts you'll need
callout.text: If you're not familiar, these three will get you through:
list: **Feed-forward network**: multiply the input by one matrix, apply an activation function, then multiply by another matrix. It's the "feed-forward network" inside each Transformer layer.
**Softmax**: turns a set of arbitrary numbers into probabilities that sum to 1.
**Perplexity**: how "confused" a language model is when predicting the next word; lower is better.

sections.h: The problem: more parameters help, but ordinary models compute every one of them

blocks.p: The paper opens by noting that when data is plentiful, adding parameters can substantially improve accuracy—this has been shown for text, images, and speech. But in ordinary deep models, every example activates the whole model; as both model size and data increase, training cost grows roughly quadratically, and hardware progress cannot keep up.

Conditional computation has been proposed before: activate only part of the network based on the input. But the paper argues that no previous work had really demonstrated major gains in model capacity, training time, or model quality, and it identifies five challenges:

list: **GPUs are good at arithmetic, bad at branching**: if every example takes a different path, the GPU slows down, so you can only switch large chunks of the network on or off.
**Batches get fragmented**: large batches amortize the cost of parameter reads and updates, but conditional computation gives each chunk only a small portion of the examples.

**Network bandwidth is the bottleneck**: a GPU cluster's compute can be thousands of times greater than its inter-machine network bandwidth, so an algorithm's compute must far exceed the data it transfers to be worthwhile.
**Extra loss terms are needed**: controlling sparsity and load balance may affect model quality.

**You need enough data**: earlier work mostly used small image datasets of at most 600,000 images. It is hard to imagine those labels carrying enough signal to train a model with millions, let alone billions, of parameters.

sections.h: The MoE layer: many experts, only a few chosen

blocks.p: An MoE layer consists of n expert networks E_{1}, …, E_{n} and a gating network G. The output is a weighted sum of the expert outputs:

parts.desc: The output of expert i. In the paper, each expert is a feed-forward network with the same architecture but its own parameters.
The weight the gate assigns to expert i. It is sparse: most weights are 0.
This expert doesn't need to be computed; that's exactly the computation saved.

plain.title: The triage desk calls only two doctors
plain.text: A layer contains many experts (E1 through E8), and the gating network G(x) is the triage desk. For each example, triage selects only the two most relevant experts to see it (dark green); the rest don't have to do anything this time. The hospital can have hundreds or thousands of doctors, but each patient costs only the time of two.

blocks.p: How does the gate become sparse? The paper adds two things to ordinary softmax gating:

formula.expr:
H(x)_{i} = (x · W_{g})_{i} + StandardNormal() · Softplus((x · W_{noise})_{i})
G(x) = Softmax( KeepTopK( H(x), k ) )

parts.desc: Each expert's score; W_{g} is a trainable matrix.
Adds a bit of Gaussian noise with a trainable scale to help with load balancing (more later).
Keeps only the k highest scores and sets the rest to −∞; after softmax they become 0.

plain.title: Score, add noise, keep only the top two
plain.text: The triage desk scores every expert, adds a little random noise (so unpopular experts occasionally get a chance), then keeps only the k highest scores (here, 2), crosses out the rest, and divides the weight among the ones left.

fig.title: Worked gate example: 8 experts, only 2 computed
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: the 8 expert scores are ours; noise is ignored; k = 2. Computed from the paper's equations (3)-(5).
fig.note: With ordinary softmax gating, every expert gets a weight, so all 8 must be computed. Top-2 gating runs softmax only over the two top-scoring experts (0.731 and 0.269), so only 2 are computed, and the expert compute drops to one quarter.

blocks.p: **How is the gating network trained?** By ordinary backpropagation, together with the rest of the model. The paper notes that as long as k > 1, the gate values of the selected experts have non-zero gradients with respect to the gate parameters. This differs from earlier work that used Boolean switches and reinforcement learning to train gates. The paper also concedes that keeping only the top k creates theoretically worrying discontinuities in the gating function, but no problem has been observed in practice.

callout.title: Like a hospital with thousands of specialists
callout.text: An ordinary network is like a single general practitioner who has to see each patient from start to finish. An MoE is like a large hospital: the triage desk (the gating network) glances at the patient and sends them only to the most relevant specialists. The hospital can employ thousands of doctors (parameters explode), but each patient only takes time from a few (compute stays flat). The hard part is ensuring triage doesn't keep sending patients to the same few doctors.

blocks.p: When there are thousands or even tens of thousands of experts, the gate itself gets expensive. The paper uses a **two-level hierarchical MoE**: a primary gate first selects several groups, and each group has its own gate to choose experts inside it.

sections.h: Making it fast: batches and bandwidth

blocks.p: **Batches get fragmented.** In a batch of b examples, each example picks k of n experts, so each expert receives only about kb / n examples on average. More experts mean smaller expert batches and less efficient GPUs.

The paper's fix is to **mix data parallelism and model parallelism**: ordinary layers and gating networks use normal data parallelism (one replica per machine), but each expert exists as a single shared copy, spread across machines. All machines run in sync, and each expert gathers the relevant examples from every machine. With d machines, each expert's batch becomes roughly kbd / n, a factor of d larger.

fig.title: Worked example: how small expert batches get, and how much mixed parallelism helps
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: the per-machine batch b, expert count n, and selected experts k are chosen by us, and calculated using the formulas in Section 3.1.
rows: Then send all the timesteps of a sentence to the MoE together (say, 20 words)
fig.note: The paper also exploits a "convolutional" application: because the same MoE is applied at every timestep, once the previous layer has finished all timesteps, they can be sent to the MoE as one large batch.

plain.title: When each expert gets too few people, carpool
plain.text: A batch spread across thousands of experts gives each expert only a few examples (A), so a GPU computing that tiny slice at a time is very wasteful. The paper has multiple machines combine the examples headed to the same expert before computing (B), like merging several cars carrying one passenger each into a single full car.

blocks.p: **Network bandwidth.** Because experts stay fixed on their machines and the gate has few parameters, communication mostly consists of moving expert inputs and outputs back and forth. To be efficient, an expert's compute relative to its input and output size must exceed the ratio of GPU compute to network bandwidth—on GPUs the paper says this can be "thousands to one." For an expert with one hidden layer, that ratio is exactly the hidden layer size, so making the hidden layer large (thousands of units) is enough.

The ambition is huge: the paper's stated goal is a trillion-parameter model trained on a trillion-word corpus. It had not reached that scale at the time of writing, but "it should be possible by adding more hardware."

sections.h: Load balancing: don't let the gate play favorites

blocks.p: The paper observes that the gating network tends to converge to always giving large weights to the same few experts. This imbalance is **self-reinforcing**: favored experts get more training, improve faster, and become even more likely to be selected.
The paper's solution is a soft constraint. It defines an expert's "importance" on a batch as the sum of its gate weights, then adds a loss that penalizes differences in importance across experts:

formula.expr:
Importance(X) = Σ_{x∈X} G(x)
L_{importance}(X) = w_{importance} · CV( Importance(X) )^{2}

parts.desc: The sum of gate weights each expert receives over a batch.
Coefficient of variation: standard deviation ÷ mean, measuring how much experts differ from one another.
A hand-tuned scaling factor; the paper uses 0.1 in the language modeling experiments.

plain.title: Don't let triage favor just one or two doctors
plain.text: If triage always sends patients to the same doctor (left), that doctor is exhausted while everyone else sits idle and learns nothing. The paper adds the imbalance in "how much weight each expert got in this batch" (CV²) to the loss: the more lopsided the distribution, the heavier the penalty, pushing triage to spread work evenly (right).

fig.title: Worked example: more imbalance, bigger penalty
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: the importance values for 4 experts over a batch are ours; CV uses the population standard deviation.

blocks.p: **Equal importance is not equal load.** One expert may receive a few examples with large weights, and another many examples with small weights; their importance can match even though the number of examples handled differs sharply, which can cause out-of-memory errors or uneven speed on distributed hardware. So the paper adds a second loss, L_{load}, that directly balances "how many examples each expert gets."

But "how many examples" is a discrete number and has no gradient. That is exactly what the **noise** in the gate is for: with noise, whether an expert is selected becomes a probability, and the normal cumulative distribution function gives a smooth estimate that can backpropagate.

fig.title: The effect of the two balancing losses
fig.subtitle: From Table 6 in the paper's appendix; the MoE-256 model trained for 10 epochs. The last column is the busiest expert's load as a multiple of the average load.
fig.note: With no balancing loss, the busiest expert's load is 17.8× the average, and perplexity is also much worse (39.8). With either loss, quality is about the same; a larger weight on the load loss makes the busiest expert's burden lighter.

blocks.p: Also, to avoid memory overflow at the start from uneven loads, the paper initializes W_{g} and W_{noise} to 0 so the gate begins with only noise and no preferences.

sections.h: Experiment 1: language modeling, with parameter count up more than 1,000×

blocks.p: **1-billion-word benchmark**: roughly 829 million words of news sentences, with a vocabulary of 793,471 words. The model stacks two LSTM layers with one MoE layer between them. Each expert is a feed-forward network with a hidden layer of 1,024 units and about 1 million parameters; each input activates 4 experts, so the MoE part does about 4 million multiply-adds per timestep, each LSTM layer about 2 million, for about 8 million total.

fig.title: With equal compute, more experts are better
fig.subtitle: From part of Table 7 in the paper's appendix, on the 1-billion-word benchmark trained for 10 epochs. Every model uses about 8 million multiply-adds per timestep.
columns: Parameters (millions, excluding word embeddings and softmax)
fig.note: The second column excludes word embeddings and the softmax layer. With compute unchanged, parameters rise from about 9.4 million to about 4.3 billion, and perplexity falls about 24%. Beyond about 1 billion parameters, though, returns diminish.

fig.title: High-capacity MoE vs. the previous best
fig.subtitle: From Table 1 of the paper. Parameters and per-timestep compute both exclude word embeddings and the softmax layer.
fig.note: The low-budget MoE beats the previous best after the same number of epochs while using only about 6% of its compute. The high-budget MoE uses comparable compute and has much lower perplexity.

blocks.p: **100-billion-word corpus**: the paper expects that with more data, added capacity will pay off even more. On roughly 100 billion words of Google-internal news, with the same compute budget of about 8 million operations per timestep, it scales experts all the way to 131,072, and the MoE layer reaches about 137 billion parameters.

fig.title: With more data, capacity matters more
fig.subtitle: From part of Table 8 in the paper's appendix; test perplexity after 1 epoch on the 100-billion-word corpus.
fig.note: At 65,536 experts (about 68 billion parameters), perplexity is 39% lower than the compute-matched baseline; each example uses only 4 of those experts, making the layer 99.994% sparse. Doubling to 131,072 experts actually makes it worse, which the paper suspects may be due to too much sparsity.

blocks.p: The paper cuts Google's GNMT translation system from 9 and 8 LSTM layers in the encoder and decoder down to 3 and 2, then inserts one MoE layer in each. Every MoE layer has up to 2,048 experts with about 2 million parameters apiece, adding roughly 8 billion parameters in total.

fig.title: Single language-pair translation: less compute, higher BLEU
fig.subtitle: From Tables 2 and 3 of the paper; WMT'14 newstest2014
fig.note: The paper reports that compared with GNMT without reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, English–French and English–German score 1.34 and 1.12 BLEU higher. On Google's internal English–French production data, test BLEU is 1.01 higher in just one-sixth of the training time.

blocks.p: **Multilingual translation**: one model handles 12 language pairs at once. A previous multilingual GNMT underperformed 12 separate models—no surprise, since together they had 12 times the capacity. With MoE, perplexity drops 19% below multilingual GNMT, BLEU improves on 11 of the 12 language pairs (by up to 5.84 points), and 8 even beat the individually trained models. The sole decline is English→Korean, which the paper attributes to overfitting from oversampling a scarce language pair's small set of real examples.

**Experts really do specialize.** The paper lists the contexts most often handled by several experts in the English–French translation model's encoder: one handles words like "innovation, researcher"; one handles the indefinite article "a" in "play an important role"; one handles words meaning "fast." The division of labor is learned, not imposed.

list: **The translation experiments don't use the main gating network.** Appendix F notes that due to particular infrastructure circumstances at the time (later fixed), the single-language-pair translation experiments used a "strictly balanced" gate: within each batch, every expert takes only a fixed number of the highest-scoring examples, and at inference a learned threshold approximates it. The noisy Top-K gate from the main text is used only for language modeling and multilingual translation.

**The "18% lower" is about 19% by the table.** Appendix C.2 says the high-budget MoE's perplexity after 10 epochs is 18% lower than the previous best; plugging in the 28.0 and 34.7 from the table gives about 19%.

**Efficiency isn't always high**: the largest 131,072-expert model reaches only 0.30 TFLOPS per GPU, far below the other models. The paper explains that it deliberately did not scale the batch size with the number of GPUs, to keep the comparison fair.

**A typo**: Section 1.3 says the goal is to turn MoE into a tool for "computational computation"; from context it should be "conditional computation." This arXiv version still says "under review," and it contains several similar spelling errors.

**Theoretical concerns are set aside.** The discontinuity introduced by keeping only the top k, and the gate gradient flowing only to selected experts, are addressed only with the paper's statement that no problem was observed in practice; there is no deeper analysis.

sections.h: Afterward: from LSTM to Transformer, to today's large models

list: **A memory-saving optimizer.** To fit up to 1 billion parameters on each GPU, the paper modifies Adam: it drops the first moment (setting β_{1} = 0) and approximates the second-moment matrix with two vectors—the row means and column means. The paper notes that Adam's two moment estimates would triple memory usage (see the Adam close read). This idea later became the Adafactor optimizer, used to train T5 (see the T5 close read).

**Moving into the Transformer.** Later work replaces each Transformer layer's feed-forward network with an MoE layer. The next paper on this path, **Switch Transformer**, simplifies k to 1: each token goes to only one expert, pushing scale past a trillion parameters.

**Today's mainstream large models.** DeepSeek-V3 has 671 billion total parameters, but each token activates only about 37 billion of them—exactly the idea of decoupling total parameters from compute (see the DeepSeek-R1 close read). Load balancing remains one of the central design problems in these models.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you get it?

quiz.q: Why can MoE make parameter count explode while compute stays nearly flat?
options: The gating network selects only k experts to compute for each input; the others have weight 0 and are never computed.
quiz.why: Total parameters grow with the number of experts, but each input only goes through k experts. In the paper, 65,536 experts have only 4 used per example, making the layer 99.994% sparse.

quiz.q: Why add noise to the gating network?
options: To help load balancing: with noise, "whether an expert is selected" becomes a differentiable probability, which allows a smooth load loss.
quiz.why: "How many examples an expert gets" is discrete and cannot backpropagate. With noise, the probability of being selected can be written using the normal cumulative distribution function, and summing those probabilities gives a differentiable load estimate.

quiz.q: What happens without any load-balancing loss?
options: The gate increasingly favors a few experts, which is self-reinforcing. In the paper's experiments, the busiest expert's load was about 18× the average, and perplexity was also worse.
quiz.why: Favored experts train more, get better, and become even more likely to be selected. In Table 6 of the paper, perplexity without the loss is 39.8; adding either loss lowers it to about 35.6–35.7.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: What tension does conditional computation try to resolve? Why hadn't it succeeded before?
How is the noisy Top-K gate computed?
Why does each expert's batch get smaller as expert count grows, and how does the paper solve it?
Why make the expert hidden layers larger?
What do the importance loss and load loss each balance?
How does dataset size affect the gains from MoE?
How did the MoE idea later make its way into the Transformer and today's large models?
